sentences.text: A lower rate cuts the monthly payment.
But the refinance has a price, and the savings must repay it first.
So how far do rates have to fall before a refinance pays for itself?
This is a lab for money decisions: we run the numbers on public data and show every assumption.
US only. The rates here are history, not a forecast.
By the end, you will see the exact rate drop that repays a typical refinance within 36 months, and how every rate drop since 1971 actually played out.
Here is the rate itself: the weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage, from Freddie Mac's survey.
It peaked at 18.63% in 1981.
It bottomed at 2.65% in 2021.
Every fall in that line is a moment when homeowners asked the same question.
First question, then: what does a refinance actually cost?
Lenders report it for every loan they make, under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, as total loan costs.
Those are the closing costs: origination charges, discount points, the appraisal, title insurance, and the rest.
Discount points are optional: paying more at closing buys a lower rate, so part of that bill is a choice.
Cash-out refinances, which also take equity out of the house, cost more: a median of $8,655. This film keeps to refinances that change only the rate and the term.
In 2025, lenders reported 488,241 of those, into 30-year first mortgages.
In nominal dollars, the median one cost $5,124.
The middle half paid between $3,443 and $8,270.
The count follows the rate. In 2021, near the bottom, lenders reported 3,089,298 of them.
Their median bill that year was $3,406.
But the dollar figure hides the real pattern. The bill barely grows with the size of the loan.
On loans under $150,000, the median cost was 3.4% of the amount borrowed.
On loans of $750,000 and more, it was 0.5%.
So the same cut in rate repays a large loan faster than a small one. Keep that in mind; it comes back.
Paying the bill back is simple division: the closing costs, divided by the drop in the monthly payment.
The answer is the break-even: the month when the savings have covered the bill.
Before that month, the refinance is still in the red. After it, every payment is money kept.
Now the main question: how big does the drop have to be?
Take the median refinance: a balance of $375,000, and $5,124 to close.
Say the old loan carries 7.62%, the average rate in the month the last big drop began, October 2023.
Cut the rate by 0.25 points, and the payment falls by $64 a month.
At that pace, the bill takes 80 months to come back.
Double the cut to 0.5 points, and the payment falls by $128 a month.
Break-even arrives in 41 months.
A cut of 1 point saves $253 a month.
That pays back the bill in 21 months.
2 points pay back in 11 months, well inside a year.
Look at the shape of that curve. It is not a straight line.
Below 0.5 points it climbs steeply: each smaller cut adds years, not months.
That is where the common rule of thumb about a full point comes from: for this loan, 1 point pays back in 21 months, 0.5 points in 41.
But remember the pattern in the costs, and move the same question to a different loan.
To break even within 36 months, the median loan needs a cut of 0.56 points.
A loan under $150,000 needs 1.32 points, because its bill is a bigger share of the balance.
A loan of $750,000 or more needs only 0.2.
Give the median loan 60 months instead, and 0.33 points is enough.
Give it 84 months, and it needs 0.24.
Read each of those as a flip point: below it, the bill outlasts the stay; above it, the savings win.
So there is no single threshold. The drop that pays back depends on two things: how big the loan is, and how long it is kept.
And how long it is kept is the one number no dataset can supply.
One more cost hides inside the new loan. It starts a fresh 30 years, so the last payment moves further away, even when each payment is smaller.
The simple division ignores that. It answers only the first question: when do the savings cover the bill?
The division assumes the new rate is the last one. What happened in the real drops?
We found every fall of at least 1 point in the 30-year rate since 1971: 13 of them.
In each, a borrower who took a loan at the peak refinances in the first month the rate is 1 point lower.
Closing costs use the median share for that year; before 2018, lenders did not report them, so a fixed share is used and marked illustrative.
The steepest falls came in the early 1980s.
After the peak of 1981, the first cut of 1 point came 2 months later.
It paid back in 13 months, but the slide went on, and the next point came 9 months after the refinance.
Some drops were brief. The fall that began in 1987 lasted 4 months, and the refinance came at its very bottom.
The drop that began in 2006 was slower. The refinance came in January 2008, and it had paid for itself before the next point arrived.
At a cut of 1 point, break-even took between 10 and 21 months across all 13 drops.
But in 5 of them, the rate kept falling: another drop of 1 point before the first refinance had paid for itself.
Those borrowers met the same question twice, and a second refinance starts a new clock with a new bill.
In the drop that began in November 2018, the refinance came in June 2019.
It needed 18 months to break even, and the next drop of 1 point came only 17 months later.
In the other 8, the first refinance was the one that mattered.
The latest drop began in October 2023. The cut of 1 point arrived in August 2024.
At that year's median cost, it paid back in 21 months.
So, how far do rates have to fall before a refinance pays for itself?
For the median loan and median costs, a cut that repays it within 36 months is 0.56 points.
Half as much patience asks for more: to pay back in 21 months takes 1 point.
That answer has limits. It counts payment savings only: no taxes, no return on the cash, and a new 30-year loan restarts the clock on owning the house outright.
It uses medians: half of borrowers paid more than $5,124, and an offered rate can differ from the survey average.
And it is history, not a forecast: nothing here says where rates go next.
What history does show is the shape of the trade: a known bill up front, against savings that arrive one month at a time, for as long as the loan lasts.
Method. Rates are Freddie Mac's weekly survey via FRED, checked against the Optimal Blue index since 2017.
A drop counts when the monthly average falls at least 1 point from a peak before rising 1 point from its low.
Costs are HMDA loan-level data from 2018 to 2025: originated refinances, first lien, 30-year term.
Closing costs are paid in cash, with no taxes and no discounting. Every figure and formula is listed in the description.
A small cut needs a long stay. A large loan needs a smaller cut. And a falling rate can make the first refinance too early.
The break-even is simple division. The hard part is the number only the borrower knows: how long the loan will be kept.
The bill is known the day the loan closes. The savings arrive one month at a time.
The sources are linked in the description, and the next decision is already on the bench.
